extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates learning schemes and algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation, construction, and practical computation of fibered products (base change/pullbacks) of schemes, including conceptual (functorial) perspective, gluing/affine reductions, and examples of fibers. Includes warnings about pathologies and guidance for computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of fibered products
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 9.1.1: Suppose α : X → Z and β : Y → Z are morphisms of schemes. Then the fibered product X ×_Z Y exists in the category of schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary existence statement. The rest of §9.1 gives warnings, several constructions (affine case, gluing), and two complementary proofs (concrete gluing of affines and representable-functor perspective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of schemes are not products of underlying sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning 9.1.2: The product of schemes (and more generally fibered products) need not coincide with the product of underlying sets; constructing a scheme product naively on underlying sets yields incorrect behavior (extra points can appear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A1_k ×_k A1_k ≅ A2_k, but the underlying set of A2_k contains extra points (corresponding to curves) not present if one took a naive set-theoretic product. Don't attempt to construct scheme products by first taking set-theoretic/topological products.

rubrics_metrics.name: W-valued points and Yoneda universal property
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 9.1.3 / (9.1.3.1): For any scheme W, Hom(W, X ×_Z Y) = Hom(W, X) ×_{Hom(W,Z)} Hom(W, Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functor-of-points identity justifies defining scheme-valued points and is the universal property that characterizes fibered products. Use Yoneda's lemma / functor-of-points language to reason about fibered products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherianness need not be preserved under base change
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning 9.1.4: The fibered product of Noetherian schemes need not be Noetherian (pathology example given via tensor products); however, the fibered product of finite type k-schemes over finite type k-schemes is finite type over k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume Noetherian property is stable under arbitrary base change. For varieties (finite type over a field) the pathology does not occur; check hypotheses carefully when transferring finiteness/Noetherian properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine fibered product via tensor product
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 9.1.B: Given ring maps C → A and C → B, Spec(A ⊗_C B) ≅ Spec A ×_{Spec C} Spec B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On affines, fibered products reduce to tensor products of rings. Interpret tensor product as the 'fibered coproduct' in the category of rings. This is the fundamental computational tool for affine cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gluing affines and open embeddings to build fibered products
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy 9.1.5 and proof steps: Because schemes are glued from affines along open subsets, construct fibered products by taking affine fibered products locally and gluing via open embeddings (which are preserved by fibered product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: cover target by affines, take preimages, compute affinely, then glue using uniqueness of morphisms and compatibility on overlaps. Key facts used repeatedly: schemes glue (Exercise 4.4.A) and morphisms glue (Exercise 6.3.A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representable-functor perspective on fibered products
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.1.6: The statement 'X ×_Z Y exists' translates to 'h_X ×_{h_Z} h_Y is representable', where h_X is the functor Mor(·, X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thinking in terms of representable functors clarifies the universal property: construct the functor-of-points fibered product and then show it is representable by a scheme. This viewpoint can make conceptual arguments cleaner after absorbing the concrete proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representable functors must be Zariski sheaves (necessary condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.1.7: If a functor is representable then the functor h_X is a Zariski sheaf (morphisms glue on open covers), so being a Zariski sheaf is necessary for representability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equalizer exact sequences to check the sheaf condition. This gives a necessary test for representability of a functor on Sch (or Sch_S).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibered product of representable functors is a Zariski sheaf
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 9.1.D: For schemes X, Y, Z, the functor h_X ×_{h_Z} h_Y is a Zariski sheaf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use representability to prove this; rather verify the sheaf property directly for the fibered product of functors. This is one ingredient in proving representability via local representability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local representability implies representability (gluing representables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key Exercise 9.1.I: If a functor h is a Zariski sheaf and has an open cover by representable functors (i.e., is 'covered by schemes'), then h is representable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glue the schemes representing the open subfunctors using Exercise 4.4.A. This result is used to deduce existence of X ×_Z Y from the fact that h_X ×_{h_Z} h_Y is a Zariski sheaf and is locally representable by affines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four atomic types for computing base change / fibered products
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.2 intro: There are four types of morphisms particularly easy to take fibered products with: (1) base change by open embeddings, (2) adding extra variables, (3) closed embeddings (quotients), (4) localization. All morphisms can be built from these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To compute A ⊗_B C in practice, reduce to adding variables and taking quotients; localization (4) is also frequently useful. This gives a practical recipe for constructing fibered products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding variables: tensor with polynomial ring
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.2.A: A ⊗_B B[t] ≅ A[t], so forming the fibered product with B[t] corresponds to adding an extra variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this when the map is 'add variable' type; the universal property of polynomial rings shows the isomorphism. This can be extended to adding infinitely many variables if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base change by closed embeddings corresponds to quotient by extended ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.2.B / 9.2.2: If φ: B → A is a ring morphism and I ⊂ B an ideal, then A ⊗_B (B/I) ≅ A / I_e where I_e is the extension of I to A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, the fibered product with a closed subscheme is a closed subscheme of the fibered product; 'closed embeddings are preserved by base change.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersections of (locally) closed embeddings realized as fibered products
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.2.C: The intersection of two closed embeddings into X may be interpreted as their fibered product over X; locally closed embeddings and finite intersections are preserved under base change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fibered product formalism to define scheme-theoretic intersections; show preservation under base change and that intersections of finitely many locally closed embeddings remain locally closed embeddings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization and base change: localization commutes with tensor product
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.2.F: Given φ: B → A and a multiplicative subset S ⊂ B, φ(S)^{-1}A ≅ A ⊗_B (S^{-1}B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal translation: the fibered product with a localization is the localization of the fibered product in the obvious way. Useful when taking distinguished opens or generic points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Important monomorphisms: open embeddings, closed embeddings, localizations
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.2.G: Open embeddings, closed embeddings, and localization of affine schemes are monomorphisms in Sch; monomorphisms are closed under composition, so compositions (e.g., locally closed embeddings, maps from Spec of stalks) are monomorphisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: certain monomorphisms (e.g., Spec O_{X,p} → X) are not open embeddings in general. Use this when reasoning about uniqueness or injectivity properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine/projective spaces pull back from Spec Z
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.2.H: A^n_A ≅ A^n_Z ×_{Spec Z} Spec A and P^n_A ≅ P^n_Z ×_{Spec Z} Spec A; affine and projective spaces over A are pulled back from their universal manifestations over Spec Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses that these standard schemes are functorially obtained by base change from universal objects over Spec Z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending base field and descent of properties
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.2.6 and Exercises 9.2.I–J: Given a k-scheme X and a field extension ℓ/k, base changing X to ℓ (X_ℓ = X ×_{Spec k} Spec ℓ) is a fundamental operation: many properties can be checked after base change (and some descend back). For example, equality of two morphisms and being a closed embedding descend from ℓ to k under appropriate hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use base extension to reduce to algebraically closed or simpler fields when checking properties; verify descent hypotheses before concluding properties for the original scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: fibered product as pulling back families
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.3.1: If Y → Z is a family of schemes parametrized by Z and ψ: X → Z, then X ×_Z Y is the pulled-back family of Y parametrized by X (scheme-theoretic inverse image).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology: 'pullback', 'base change', 'inverse image scheme', 'pullback diagram' or 'base change diagram'. Use this geometric intuition to interpret constructions (e.g., setting parameter t to a value corresponds to base change to Spec k[t]/(t−a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibers of a morphism defined via base change to residue fields
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.3.2: For g: Y → Z and a point p ∈ Z with residue field K and chosen map Spec K → Z, the scheme-theoretic fiber g^{-1}(p) is Y ×_Z Spec K. If Z is irreducible, the fiber over the generic point is the generic fiber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute fibers by localizing and taking quotients in affine coordinates (localization + closed embedding trick). Be precise about the chosen map Spec K → Z when dealing with non-closed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: General fiber vs generic fiber; notion of 'general' and 'generic'
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.3.6: 'General fiber' means fibers over points in a dense open subset of Y have a property; 'generic fiber' means the fiber over the generic point (requires Y irreducible). These notions differ: general ⇒ generic but not conversely in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In good situations (Y irreducible Noetherian, π finite type), properties of the generic fiber often extend to a dense open (use Chevalley, etc.). State hypotheses when promoting generic information to general fibers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphisms have finite fibers
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.3.4 remark: If π is finite then its fibers are finite (exercise 7.3.K).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an important general fact to use when analyzing fiber cardinalities; consult earlier exercises for proof and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generically finite morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: 9.3.6: For π: X → Y finite type, π is generically finite if after base change to the generic point of each irreducible component, π becomes finite (equivalently, the preimage of the generic point is finite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a useful intermediate finiteness notion; check either condition depending on context (base-change-to-generic-point or preimage cardinality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: fibers of y^2 = x over Q illustrate multiple fiber phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Example 9.3.3: For the morphism Spec Q[x,y]/(y^2−x) → Spec Q[x], fibers over x=1 (two Q-points), x=0 (one nonreduced point), x=−1 (one reduced point but of degree 2 over Q), and the generic point (degree-2 field extension) demonstrate different senses of 'counting' fiber size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this and similar examples to see how multiplicity, nonreduced structure, and residue-field extensions all contribute to perceived fiber 'size'. This motivates notions like finite flat morphisms and counting with multiplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up example: Bl(0,0) A^2_k and its exceptional divisor
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 9.3.F: Define the closed subscheme Bl(0,0) A^2_k ⊂ A^2_k ×_k P^1_k cut out by xv = yu (with affine coords u,v on A^2_k and projective coords on P^1_k). The fiber over (0,0) is the exceptional divisor (an effective Cartier divisor), and away from (0,0) the morphism is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concrete description provides an explicit pullback/construction example (useful for visual intuition about blow-ups): blow-up replaces a point by P^1, and the exceptional divisor is locally cut out by a single non-zerodivisor.
